title: Cannes 2026 Is Over. A Romanian Film About Norway Won. Here's Every Prize, Every Surprise, and What India Actually Got Out of It.
excerpt: Cristian Mungiu's Fjord took the Palme d'Or in a shock decision. No Indian film competed for a major prize. But Payal Kapadia ran a jury, a Nepali film won, and an FTII student made the official selection. The full picture is more interesting than any single award.
body:
The 79th Cannes Film Festival wrapped tonight with a closing ceremony that honoured Barbra Streisand with an Honorary Palme d'Or and handed the top prize to a film almost nobody predicted.

Fjord, a Romanian-Norwegian co-production about a clash of cultures in a tiny Norwegian town, won the Palme d'Or for director Cristian Mungiu. It's his second — he won in 2007 for the shattering abortion drama 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days. Few saw this coming. The critical conversation had been dominated by Pawel Pawlikowski's Fatherland and Andrey Zvyagintsev's Minotaur.

The Full Winners List

Palme d'Or: Fjord — Cristian Mungiu (Romania/Norway/Denmark/France/Sweden)

Grand Prix: Minotaur — Andrey Zvyagintsev (France/Latvia/Germany)

Jury Prize: The Dreamed Adventure — Valeska Grisebach (Germany/France/Austria/Bulgaria)

Best Director (tied): Javier Ambrossi & Javier Calvo for The Black Ball, and Pawel Pawlikowski for Fatherland

Best Actress (tied): Virginie Efira and Tao Okamoto for All of a Sudden (Ryusuke Hamaguchi)

Best Actor: Emmanuel Macchia and Valentin Campagne for Coward (Lukas Dhont)

Best Screenplay: Emmanuel Marre for A Man of His Time

Un Certain Regard Prize: Everytime — Sandra Wollner

Un Certain Regard Jury Prize: Elephants in the Fog — Abinash Bikram Shah (Nepal)

Caméra d'Or: Ben'Imana — Marie Clémentine Dusabejambo (Rwanda)

Short Film Palme d'Or: For the Opponents — Federico Luis

Where Was India?

No Indian film competed in the main competition — again. But India's presence at Cannes was more substantive than the typical red-carpet photo-op coverage would suggest.

Payal Kapadia ran a jury. Just two years after winning the Grand Prix for All We Imagine as Light, the Indian filmmaker served as jury president of the Critics' Week section. That's a position of genuine institutional power — she decided which debut films got the section's top prize.

Nepal made history. Elephants in the Fog by Abinash Bikram Shah — a film about trans women — won the Un Certain Regard Jury Prize. It's the first time Nepal has ever won a prize at Cannes. The film is a Nepal-France-Germany-Brazil-Norway co-production, and its success points to the growing visibility of South Asian stories outside India's shadow.

An FTII student made the official selection. Mehar Malhotra's 24-minute Punjabi-language film was one of only two Indian entries in Cannes' official programming, screened in the La Cinef (formerly Cinéfondation) section.

Supriya Pathak announced her directorial debut. The veteran actress used Cannes to reveal Our Story, a film about three generations of women in her own family, co-produced between India and Australia.

What NRIs Should Take Away

For diaspora cinephiles, this year's Cannes tells a familiar story with new texture. India still isn't breaking through to the main competition in the way that South Korea, Japan, or even Romania does consistently. But the ecosystem is diversifying. Kapadia's jury role suggests institutional respect. The FTII selection shows pipeline potential. Nepal's win expands what "South Asian cinema at Cannes" even means.

The 22-film main competition was dominated by European auteurs — Mungiu, Zvyagintsev, Pawlikowski, Hamaguchi, Kore-eda, Almodóvar, Farhadi. To compete here, India needs filmmakers who can access European co-production money and distribution networks while telling stories that travel.

Payal Kapadia did exactly that. Whether more will follow depends on whether the Indian film industry sees Cannes as a vanity project or a genuine career path.

The Streisand Moment

Barbra Streisand received an Honorary Palme d'Or during the closing ceremony, presented by Isabelle Huppert. Peter Jackson and John Travolta also received honorary Palmes earlier in the festival. Tilda Swinton presented the main Palme d'Or.

The jury was led by Park Chan-wook and included Demi Moore, Chloé Zhao, and Stellan Skarsgård. They clearly favoured quiet, culturally textured dramas over spectacle — a choice that will be debated for months.
nri_angle: Cannes remains the single most powerful film festival for international cinema. For NRI audiences who follow global film culture, this year's results show India's growing peripheral influence — a jury presidency, student selections, debut announcements — even as the main competition remains elusive.
author: Diaspora Desk
